explanation: In Hindu-influenced Indian culture, touch customs around the head run in both directions: a younger person touching an elder's or guru's feet (charan sparsh) is a request for blessing, and an elder placing a hand on a younger person's head in return is understood as giving a blessing (ashirvad) — this is normal and welcome. A casual head-pat from a peer, stranger, or anyone outside that elder role is a different matter and can come across as condescending, especially toward an adult.
local_tip: Only touch someone's head if you're in an elder or parental role blessing a child or much younger relative; otherwise avoid it, even with kids you don't know well.

also_check.note: The head is considered the most sacred part of the body; touching it, even a child's, is a significant taboo regardless of who does it.
Patting a child's head is often seen as affectionate, but doing the same to an adult can come across as patronizing.
Patting someone on the head is generally seen as playful or affectionate, especially with children or close friends.
